items.passage: Bees and other pollinators often encounter pesticides while collecting nectar and pollen from agricultural crops. Widely used to protect crops, pesticides are toxic to insects and have contributed to population declines in all bee species. One way that bees might be able to avoid pesticides is using their incredibly good sense of taste, which can detect subtle differences between sugary solutions. Therefore, if pesticides taste bitter to them, bumblebees may be able to avoid feeding on treated crops. However, it was not clear whether bees can taste pesticides at all. Previous studies investigating a group of pesticides called neonicotinoids gave contradictory results, and explicit behavioural tests of their ability to taste pesticides had not been performed. Comparisons of neuron responses within the structures used for detecting taste showed that responses were the same whether the sugar solution contained pesticides or not.
choices: effects of neonicotinoids on the nervous systems of crops
the failure of taste as a defence against pesticides
methods for measuring sweetness in sugary solutions
reasons why pesticides are applied to flowering crops
differences in taste sensitivity among pollinator species

items.passage: One way that bees might be able to avoid pesticides is using their incredibly good sense of taste, which can detect subtle differences between sugary solutions. However, it was not clear whether bees can taste pesticides at all, and previous studies gave contradictory results. Experiments with a group of pesticides known as cholinergic showed that neuron responses were the same whether the sugar solution contained pesticides or not. Secondly, bees offered both pure and pesticide-laced sugar solutions would still drink the pesticide solution, even when it was toxic enough to make them very ill or kill them. This was the case regardless of which pesticide was used. The experiments showed that bumblebees cannot use their sense of taste to avoid drinking pesticide-laced nectar, which is an important finding for policymakers making decisions about the use of pesticides on agricultural crops.
choices: Bitter or Sweet? How Bees Rank Sugary Solutions
A Sense of Taste That Cannot Save the Bees
Neonicotinoids: The Chemistry Behind Crop Protection
Why Pollination Still Depends on Wild Insects
Designing Crops That No Longer Need Pollinators
